To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the octopus is a model for the embodiment concept, and that the octopus' nervous system is an example of how nervous systems can be organized in relation to their body.

the nervous system is not an isolated organ but an integral part of the whole organism, and that the body is not a static structure but an integral part in the continuous dynamical interactions with the environment.

the evolution of nervous systems is a consequence of the evolution of body morphology and the evolution of the environment, which together determine the constraints on the nervous system, and that nervous system organization is a result of the interaction of the four components of the embodied system.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how nervous systems evolve in relationship to their embodiment, using the octopuses and the molluscs as a leading example.
the question of what makes a nervous system efficient in the context of its embodiment.
the question of how the octopus' body plan, its nervous system, and its behavior have coevolved to produce an organism capable of complex behavior.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the octopus is a good example of how an embodied organization is a useful concept to understand how nervous systems and body morphology evolve in relation to each other and to their environment.
the octopus is an embodiment of the embodied organization concept.
octopuses are a perfect example for the embodiment concept.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the evolution of the octopus' body plan has led to an embodiment that has allowed the development of a nervous system that is able to control its body in a flexible and adaptive way, allowing it to be the most intelligent invertebrate.
the octopus' nervous system has evolved to control the octopus body, not to control the octopuses behavior.
nervous systems are the result of the evolution of a body, rather than the other way round.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can use the embodied organization approach to better understand the evolution and development, and the interaction, of the four elements that make up the octopus' nervous system and body plan.

we should not only consider the brain as the controller but also consider the mechanical system and the environment in order to understand how the nervous system has evolved in relation to the body plan.
the embodiment concept is a powerful approach for studying nervous system evolution and development in general, and for the octopus in particular.
